extracted.intended_audience: SNL fans and general pop-culture readers
extracted.subtask_description: A list-style entertainment article enumerating specific reasons why individual Saturday Night Live cast members were fired or dismissed, with short anecdotes and context for each case.

rubrics_metrics.name: Refusal to perform racially stereotypical sketches
rubrics_metrics.description: Chris Rock would flat-out refuse sketches that would have him as an African tribesman or other stereotypical roles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article cites Rock's principled refusal to play racially stereotypical parts as a reason he was let go in 1995 (along with others). It frames this as a creative and ethical disagreement with sketch content rather than poor performance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Being part of a management-initiated cast purge
rubrics_metrics.description: Louis-Dreyfus was let go as part of a vast cast purge in 1985 when Lorne Michaels returned to the show.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dismissals can occur not for individual failures but because new leadership reshuffles the cast; the article links such purges to larger production decisions and changes in show direction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dropping profanity (the "f-bomb") on live TV
rubrics_metrics.description: Charles Rocket dropped "the f-bomb" on live TV in 1981; censors were strict and SNL was fined, and Rocket was fired.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Violating broadcast decency standards in a live sketch (notably explicit profanity) is presented as a clear, actionable reason for termination, with the additional consequence of network fines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hired during a chaotic season / organizational failure
rubrics_metrics.description: Laurie Metcalf lasted just five days because the new writers and producers couldn't make the season work; the show was a 'mess.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Timing and overall show instability can doom even talented hires. The article uses Metcalf's very short tenure to show that chaotic production environments can lead to rapid dismissals unrelated to individual merit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Perceived underutilization or redundancy of a performer's specialty
rubrics_metrics.description: Jay Pharoah claims that with Obama leaving office, SNL didn't need his impression anymore and he was underutilized.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A performer's particular skill (e.g., a signature impression) can become less relevant to the show's needs, leading to dismissal; this can be framed as mutual or managerial decisions about casting utility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Performer not ready / not funny enough for the show
rubrics_metrics.description: Sarah Silverman admits she 'wasn't ready for the big time' and that she just wasn't funny enough for SNL at that point.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Self-admitted lack of readiness or not meeting the show's comedic standards is cited as a reason for being let go; the article frames this as a developmental issue rather than scandal or misconduct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Perceived mismatch where a performer is 'too talented' for the ensemble
rubrics_metrics.description: Michaela Watkins claims Lorne Michaels felt she was 'too talented' to be on the show and she was let go after one year.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article reports the unusual rationale that extreme individual talent or style can clash with ensemble needs or show tone, producing a dismissal that's counterintuitive (i.e., 'too good' to fit).

rubrics_metrics.name: Past offensive/racist material discovered (pre-hire firing)
rubrics_metrics.description: Shane Gillis was hired but videos surfaced of his history of making racist jokes; SNL let him go before he did a single episode.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Public revelation of prior offensive material or controversial past behavior can lead to immediate dismissal or rescinded hires; the article suggests better vetting could have prevented the situation.

rubrics_metrics.name: On-screen incidents compounded by executive dislike / interpersonal fit
rubrics_metrics.description: Jenny Slate dropped an 'F-bomb' on one episode, but she says her dismissal was based on Lorne Michaels allegedly feeling she didn't fit in on the show.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The piece distinguishes between a visible on-air incident and the more decisive factor of interpersonal fit with show leadership; both can operate together to cause a firing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Not fitting the season's style / lack of suitability for sketch comedy
rubrics_metrics.description: Robert Downey Jr. 'didn't click' and admits sketch comedy was never his forte; he was let go after a season often cited as among the worst.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A performer's inherent strengths may not align with sketch comedy demands or a season's creative direction; lack of fit with the medium/format is a recurring reason for dismissal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bad backstage attitude / rubbing executives the wrong way
rubrics_metrics.description: The article notes 'attitudes and some actors rubbing Lorne Michaels & NBC execs the wrong way' as recurrent problems backstage that contribute to firings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: General interpersonal behavior, attitude, and relationships with producers/executives are framed as informal but powerful factors in casting decisions; poor backstage conduct can lead to termination even without on-air failings.
